title: Oscar and the Protocol
premise: Vesper Galloway, a clone who inherited her original's unsolved murder case, works the courier route between two human worlds that severed contact decades ago. When a derelict ship returns from deep space carrying its entire crew aged backward into childhood, Vesper realizes someone has been using cryosleep to rewrite people—and that her original's murder is tied to the experiment. As the fleet's fragile truce expires and both worlds race to control the de-aging technology, Vesper must choose which half of humanity wakes first from cryosleep: the originals or their clones. She ends the cycle by destroying the protocol's master archive and broadcasting the truth of her own murder to both worlds, accepting arrest so that neither side can claim victory.
about_author: Ada Voss is the pen name of a former maritime radio operator who spent eleven years relaying messages between ships that were legally forbidden to speak to each other. They write near-future science fiction about people who keep systems running after the institutions behind them have failed.

chapters.title: The Long Route
chapters.summary: Vesper pilots a courier ship through the silence corridor between the worlds Meridian and Halcyon, smuggling letters between families split by the embargo. Through her POV we learn she is Vesper Galloway's second iteration, licensed to finish the dead woman's cases. Emotional beat: weary competence masking grief.

chapters.title: Inheritance of Dust
chapters.summary: Vesper reviews her original's final case file: a whistleblower named Ivo Renk who vanished before testifying about fleet cryogenics. Her handler, Ostrander, pressures her to close it as cold. Flashbacks show how clones inherit memories but not certainty. Beat: the ache of living someone else's unfinished life.

chapters.title: A Ship That Sailed Younger
chapters.summary: Vesper intercepts a distress ping: the deep-space vessel Anthea, missing for thirty years, drifting at the corridor's edge. Boarding it, she finds forty crew members biologically aged eight years old, healthy, terrified, and remembering adulthood. Beat: wonder curdling into dread.

chapters.title: Children Who Remember Drowning
chapters.summary: POV shifts to Maret, the Anthea's former chief engineer, now a child piloting her own body badly. She describes the Protocol: a cryosleep modification that rebuilds cells backward. The children beg Vesper not to report them—both worlds would weaponize them. Beat: protective instinct against duty.

chapters.title: Two Flags on One Hull
chapters.summary: Meridian and Halcyon patrol ships both answer the Anthea's ping. Vesper hides the children in the cargo hold and plays the two patrols against each other with forged transponders. Beat: the thrill of the long con, and the realization that invisibility is ending.

chapters.title: Ostrander's Ledger
chapters.summary: Back at Meridian station, Vesper discovers Ostrander funded the Anthea's original mission; her original was murdered to bury the connection. Loyalty to the agency that raised her collides with the evidence in her hands. Beat: betrayal by the only parent she had.

chapters.title: The Truce Clock
chapters.summary: Fleet-wide broadcast: the Meridian–Halcyon truce expires in ninety days unless a joint scientific achievement forces renewal. Both governments quietly begin hunting the Anthea. Vesper realizes the children are the bargaining chip neither side will leave unclaimed. Beat: closing walls.

chapters.title: Maret's Map
chapters.summary: Maret reveals the Anthea hid a backup of the Protocol aboard a derelict relay station in the corridor—the same station where Ivo Renk made his last transmission. Vesper sees the murder case and the technology converging on one coordinate. Beat: hope with teeth.

chapters.title: What Clones Dream
chapters.summary: Quiet interlude: Vesper and the children share watch shifts; one child asks if being a copy makes her less real. Vesper confronts the memory-fragments of her original's last hours for the first time without flinching. Beat: tenderness as resistance.

chapters.title: The Man Who Wasn't Dead
chapters.summary: At the relay station they find Ivo Renk alive—aged backward too, now a child who remembers betraying his own testimony to save his daughter. He confirms Ostrander ordered the hit on Vesper's original. Beat: justice arriving in an impossible shape.

chapters.title: Cryo Bay Seven
chapters.summary: They locate the Protocol archive sealed in the station's cryo bay alongside ten thousand sleepers: half originals, half clones, frozen during the war. Waking them all would collapse both economies; waking one half is genocide by omission. Beat: the moral trap snaps shut.

chapters.title: Halcyon's Offer
chapters.summary: A Halcyon agent, Sef Adeyemi, corners Vesper with an offer: deliver the archive and Halcyon will grant the clones legal personhood. It's everything Vesper's kind has wanted—and it means dooming the originals still asleep. Beat: temptation wearing a just face.

chapters.title: Meridian's Knife
chapters.summary: Ostrander arrives with a Meridian strike team, offering Vesper full citizenship and erasure of her clone status in exchange for the children and the archive. He calls her his finest work. She refuses; the station goes hot. Beat: severing the last tie.

chapters.title: Running the Corridor Dark
chapters.summary: A chase sequence through the silence corridor as both fleets converge. Maret, in a child's body, performs an impossible manual burn to slip the Anthea through a debris shoal. Beat: found family forged under fire.

chapters.title: The Vote in the Hold
chapters.summary: Vesper puts the decision to everyone aboard: which sleepers wake, or none. The children—who are both original and rewound—argue there is no 'half' of humanity worth saving alone. The vote deadlocks on mercy. Beat: democracy failing beautifully.

chapters.title: Renk's Confession
chapters.summary: Ivo records a full confession naming Ostrander and the Protocol's architects, admitting he traded his testimony for his daughter's inclusion in the rewind trials. Vesper realizes her original died protecting this recording. Beat: the case closes itself.

chapters.title: Ninety Days, Zero Hours
chapters.summary: The truce expires mid-crisis; first shots exchange over the relay station. Vesper broadcasts Renk's confession and the Anthea's logs to both fleets simultaneously, forcing every gun to pause on the same transmission. Beat: truth as a ceasefire.

chapters.title: Which Half Wakes
chapters.summary: Climax begins: with both fleets holding fire but demanding the archive, Vesper initiates a staggered wake sequence—alternating sleeper by sleeper, original and clone together, over ten years. Neither world gets a monopoly; both get hostages to peace. Beat: audacious compromise.

chapters.title: Ostrander's Last Case
chapters.summary: Ostrander attempts to seize the bay manually; Vesper confronts him among the sleepers and chooses arrest over killing him, delivering him and the confession to a joint tribunal both worlds must honor to keep the truce alive. Beat: justice outside the law, then inside it.

chapters.title: The Archive Burns
chapters.summary: Vesper destroys the Protocol's master copy so no government can restart the experiments, keeping only the medical data needed to care for the waking sleepers and the rewound children. Maret says goodbye to the ship that made her twice. Beat: costly renunciation.

chapters.title: Sentenced to the Route
chapters.summary: The tribunal sentences Vesper to continue the courier run—now official, now carrying open mail between reconciling worlds—for the decade of staggered wakings. Her clone status is recognized, not erased. Beat: punishment as belonging.

chapters.title: First Letter Home
chapters.summary: Epilogue: five years in, Vesper delivers the corridor's millionth letter—a child's note from a rewound crew member to the family she aged away from. Vesper adds her own letter to the original Vesper Galloway, finally signing it as herself. Beat: inheritance completed, identity claimed.
